rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī likens the idolaters' invitation to Mary’s refusal of Gabriel: if she would not turn from God toward an angel, Muhammad should not turn toward idols.
rows.anchor: قالت إنى أعوذ بالرحمان منك إن كنت تقيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī invokes Abū Ḥanīfa’s position that inability to provide and acquired impotence do not establish a right to marital separation, analogizing that one should not turn from God.
rows.anchor: مذهب أبي حنيفة أنه لا يثبت حق الفرقة بالعجز عن النفقة ولا بالعنة الطارئة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since idolaters admitted that God created them, their idols cannot be partners in any form of enterprise: they contribute neither seed, care, capital, fame, nor a legitimate share.
rows.anchor: هؤلاء الكفار كانوا معترفين بأن الله خالقهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An idol cannot seize a share by force, since it is weaker than a fly and cannot create one; the claim is irrational.
rows.anchor: ما أشد جهلكم إن هذا الصنم أكثر عجزا من الذبابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every created thing directs reason to God's essence and attributes; a mosquito reveals power through its coming-to-be, knowledge through its intricate form, and will through its precise specification.
rows.anchor: لا ذرة في عالم المحدثات إلا وهي تدعو العقول إلى معرفة الذات والصفات

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: When ʿAlī asked why ʿUmar moved aside, ʿUmar said he wished to spare him embarrassment; ʿUmar replied that carrying food, his worldly sustenance, was no shame.
rows.anchor: لم تنكبت عن الطريق ؟ فقال علي : حتى لا تستحي ، فقال : وكيف أستحي من حمل ما هو غذائيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says Muhammad should openly reject the idolaters: a mosquito challenged Nimrod, while Gabriel filled Pharaoh’s mouth with clay when he claimed divinity.
rows.anchor: يا محمد إن نمروذ لما ادعى الربوبية صاح عليه البعوض بالإنكار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to say the rejection aloud makes explicit disavowal obligatory, just as a Christian's profession of Muhammad's prophethood must explicitly repudiate Christianity.
rows.anchor: فلما أوجبت على كل مكلف أن يتبرأ بصريح لسانه عن كل دين يخالف دينك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses, temperamentally stern, was told to speak gently to Pharaoh; Muhammad was told to speak sternly, signaling the depth of his mercy.
rows.anchor: وأما محمد عليه السلام فلما أرسل إلى الخلق أمر بإظهار الخشونة تنبيها على أنه في غاية الرحمة

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A report from ʿAlī assigns the vocatives to inner levels: yā addresses the soul, ayy the heart, and hā the spirit.
rows.anchor: يا نداء النفس وأي نداي القلب ، وها نداء الروح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation makes yā a call to the absent or distant, ayy a call to the present or near, and hā an attention marker.
rows.anchor: وقيل : يا نداء الغائب وأي للحاضر ، وها للتنبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Combining distant yā with near ayy reflects human estrangement and God's nearness; placing distance first blames human failure, while the final alert hā suits the sleeper-like state between life and death.
rows.anchor: معاملتك معي وفرارك عني يوجب البعد البعيد ، لكن إحساني إليك ، ووصول نعمتي إليك توجب القرب القريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī reports that al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, and Umayya ibn Khalaf proposed alternating periods of worship to end hostility and test each other's religion.
rows.anchor: الوليد بن المغيرة والعاص بن وائل والأسود بن عبد المطلب ، وأمية بن خلف ، قالوا لرسول الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah answered the proposed compromise alongside a verse asking whether the ignorant would order Muhammad to worship other than God; when read publicly, its recipients insulted him and despaired.
rows.anchor: قل أفغير الله تأمرونى أعبد أيها الجاهلون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī distinguishes the labels: this sūrah is wholly directed at the specific group, so “disbelievers” is stronger; “ignorance” can be non-blameworthy when qualified, unlike disbelief.
rows.anchor: وليس في لدنيا لفظ أشنع ولا أبشع من لفظ الكافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī contrasts this address with a past-tense address to disbelievers in another sūrah: there the scene is Judgment Day, when the Messenger is no longer sent to them and they obey; here they remain disbelievers addressed by a Messenger.
rows.anchor: الآية المذكورة في سورة لم تحزم : إنما تقال لهم يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address is to the particular negotiators who proposed alternating worship, not every unbeliever: a universal reading would require exclusions because some Jews and Christians worship God and some unbelievers later believe.
rows.anchor: وهم الذين قالوا نعبد إلهك سنة وتعبد آلهتنا سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One no-repetition reading assigns the first pair to future worship and the second pair to present worship; the imperfect after lā denotes future, while the present denial rules out secret worship from fear or hope.
rows.anchor: أن الأول للمستقبل ، والثاني للحال والدليل على أن الأول للمستقبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading reverses the time reference: the active participle in “I am not a worshipper” negates the future sense that “I am worshipping” would convey.
rows.anchor: أن تقلب الأمر فتجعل الأول للحال والثاني للاستقبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third reading says either pair could cover present or future, but each is assigned a different time to avoid redundancy; the order may follow chronology or prioritize the proposal they made.
rows.anchor: كل واحد منهما يصلح للحال وللاستقبال ، ولكنا نخص أحداها بالحال ، والثاني بالاستقبال دفعا للتكرار

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim reads the first two “mā” clauses as relative pronouns, distinguishing idols from God, and the last two as verbal nouns, distinguishing their shirk-based worship from Muhammad's certain worship.
rows.anchor: وهو اختيار أبي مسلم أن المقصود من الأولين المعبود وما بمعنى الذي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading takes the first pair as rejecting the motives behind the bargain, then the second pair as a universal rejection of their worship for every possible purpose or perspective.
rows.anchor: أن تحمل الأولى على نفي الاعبتار الذي ذكروه ، والثانية على النفي العام المتناول لجميع الجهات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the verses repeat themselves, repetition intensifies the denial because the negotiators returned repeatedly and mistook the Prophet's silence for inclination toward their faith.
rows.anchor: رجعوا إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في هذا المعنى مرارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another defense is that the Qurʾān replied at different times as proposals shifted from a month of alternating worship to a year, repeating the same answer to each.
rows.anchor: فالمشركون قالوا : استلم بعد آلهتنا حتى نؤمن بإلهك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated answer also mocks the negotiators: because they repeated the same corrupt proposal, the response repeats itself in contempt.
rows.anchor: الجواب على التكرير على وفق قولهم وهو ضرب من التهكم فإن من كرر الكلمة الواحدة لغرض فاسد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To explain “mā” for God, one view takes it as a description: Muhammad worships truth, while the opponents do not worship truth.
rows.anchor: أن المراد منه الصفة كأنه قال : لا أعبد الباطل وأنتم لا تعبدون الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second explanation makes “mā” a verbal noun in both pairs, meaning “my worship” and “your worship,” with the first pair future and the second present.
rows.anchor: أن مصدرية في الجملتين كأنه قال : لا أعبد عبادتكم ولا تعبدون عبادتي في المسقبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third answer takes “mā” as meaning “that which,” so the expression can refer to the one Muhammad worships.
rows.anchor: أن يكون ما بمعنى الذي وحينئذ يصح الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth answer says the second “mā” follows the wording of the first for syntactic consistency, as in the parallel “a wrong is requited by a wrong like it.”
rows.anchor: كقوله : { وجزاء سيئة سيئة مثلها }

rows.speaker: أهل الجبر
rows.claim: The determinists argue that God's twice-repeated prediction that they will not worship what Muhammad worships makes commanding them to believe a demand to unite opposites.
rows.anchor: احتج أهل الجبر بأنه تعالى أخبر عنهم مرتين بقوله : { ولا أنتم عابدون ما أعبد }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says emphasis can be more useful than argument when hearers are dull or the dispute is obvious; the idolater is either irrational or stubborn, so denunciation is apt.
rows.anchor: قد يكون التأكيد والتكرير أولى من ذكر الحجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The harsh opening and gentle ending fit together: Muhammad has fully warned them, and if they refuse, he asks them to leave him in peace.
rows.anchor: كأنه يقول : إني قد بالغت في تحذيركم على هذا الأمر القبيح ، وما قصرت فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although “I will never worship” sounds stronger, there is no suspicion to dispel: everyone knew Muhammad had never worshipped an idol before revelation, unlike the Companions of the Cave.
rows.anchor: قد علم كل أحد من محمد عليه السلام أنه ما كان يعبد الصنم قبل الشرع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets the verse as assigning disbelief in God to them and exclusive monotheism and sincerity to Muhammad.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : لكم كفركم بالله ولي التوحيد والإخلاص له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This wording does not permit disbelief; the Prophet was sent to prevent it. Rāzī offers a threat, a demand to stop inviting him to shirk, or a warning to remain in a destructive faith.
rows.anchor: فإنه عليه السلام ما بعث إلا للمنع من الكفر فكيف يأذن فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second interpretation takes dīn to mean reckoning: each person receives his own account, unaffected by another's deeds.
rows.anchor: أن الدين هو الحساب أي لكم حسابكم ولي حسابي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation supplies the omitted noun “reward”: you have the recompense of your religion, and I have the recompense of mine.
rows.anchor: أن يكون على تقدير حذف المضاف أي لكم جزاء دينكم ولي جزاء ديني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth interpretation takes dīn as punishment, illustrating the usage with the prohibition against pity in God's prescribed punishment.
rows.anchor: الدين العقوبة : { ولا تأخذكم بهما رأفة فى دين الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fifth interpretation takes dīn as supplication: the opponents' prayers are lost, while God answers believers and those who call upon Him.
rows.anchor: القول الخامس : الدين الدعاء ، فادعو الله مخلصين له الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sixth interpretation takes dīn as custom: their inherited habit comes from ancestors and devils, while Muhammad's comes from angels and revelation; a poetic line contrasts the two habits.
rows.anchor: الدين العادة ، قال الشاعر : يقول لها وقد دارت وضيني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is restrictive: each has only his own religion and responsibility. Muhammad must convey revelation, while the audience must accept it; he has discharged his duty, and their persistence does not harm him.
rows.anchor: قوله : { لكم دينكم } يفيد الحصر ، ومعناه لكم دينكم لا لغيركم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī rejects using this verse as a casual expression of leaving others alone: the Qurʾān was revealed for reflection and action according to its commands.
rows.anchor: جرت عادة الناس بأن يتمثلوا بهذه الآية عند المتاركة ، وذلك غير جائز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī links the three blessings to three acts in the previous sūrah: Muhammad's verbal rejection earns divine support, his heart's turn to monotheism earns Mecca's conquest, and his bodily obedience is answered by crowds entering his religion.
rows.anchor: إنك قلت في السورة المتقدمة : { قل يأيها الكافرون لا أعبد ما تعبدون }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three blessings call for three forms of servitude: glorification for victory, praise for conquest, and seeking forgiveness as many followers bring more sins and the pleasure of prestige may distract the Prophet.
rows.anchor: إن نصرتك فسبح ، وإن فتحت مكة فاحمد وإن أسلموا ، فاستغفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the Prophet's forceful disavowal and the parting formula, God reassures him that victory will come to him, rather than requiring him to travel to it.
rows.anchor: يا محمد لا تخف فإني لا أذهب بك إلى النصر بل أجيء بالنصر إليك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī treats the sūrah as a reminder that worldly ease is temporary: after completion comes decline, so the Prophet should seek forgiveness rather than grieve hardship or rejoice in prosperity.
rows.anchor: أما علمت أنه لا بد بعد الكمال من الزوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When completion is announced, one should expect decline, keeping the heart from settling on worldly life and ready for departure.
rows.anchor: توقع زوالا إذا قيل تم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prior sūrah asks about the Prophet's recompense and receives the promise of victory, while Abū Lahab's call to idol worship receives a warning; promise precedes threat because mercy precedes wrath and generosity prizes fulfilled promises.
rows.anchor: لأن رحمته سبقت غضبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī suggests the preceding sūrah avoids naming God with unbelievers, using “mā” lest they mock the name, while this sūrah names Him for the friends who honor it.
rows.anchor: أن في السورة المتقدمة لم يذكر شيئا من أسماء الله ، بل قال : ما أعبد بلفظ ما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians construe “idhā” as governed by “glorify”: when victory arrives, fill its time with glorification, praise, and forgiveness, completing the exchange of gifts and love.
rows.anchor: قال النحويون : إذا منصوب بسبح ، والتقدير فسبح بحمد ربك إذا جاء نصر الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised increase for gratitude means these acts raise Muhammad's ranks in this life and the next.
rows.anchor: فيصير اشتغالك بهذه الطاعات سببا لمزيد درجاتك في الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faith requires negation and affirmation, disavowal and allegiance: the previous sūrah supplies rejection of false worship, and this one supplies affirmation through God's victory.
rows.anchor: أن الإيمان إنما يتم بأمرين : بالنفي والإثبات وبالبراءة والولاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One distinction is that victory is aid toward a goal and opening is attainment of the goal; thus victory is a cause and conquest its result.
rows.anchor: النصر هو الإعانة على تحصيل المطلوب ، والفتح هو تحصيل المطلوب الذي كان متعلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another distinction makes victory the completion of religion and opening the worldly flourishing that completes the blessing, like the verse pairing perfected religion with completed favor.
rows.anchor: النصر كمال الدين ، والفتح الإقبال الدنيوي الذي هو تمام النعمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third distinction makes victory worldly triumph and opening entry into Paradise; Rāzī says the clearest meaning is triumph over Quraysh or all the Arabs.
rows.anchor: وأظهر الأقوال في النصر أنه الغلبة على قريش أو على جميع العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though Muhammad was always aided by proofs and miracles, this “victory” is the natural, worldly triumph of Mecca; its significance makes earlier aid seem absent, or it is the worldly victory promised to prophets.
rows.anchor: المراد من هذا النصر هو النصر الموافق للطبع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling it God's victory can mean a victory uniquely fitting God's wisdom, a master craftsman's work attributed to its famous maker, or the answer to believers' plea for help.
rows.anchor: معناه نصر لا يليق إلا بالله ولا يليق أن يفعله إلا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Victory comes” personifies a divinely appointed event: every occurrence has fixed causes and a time that cannot advance or be delayed.
rows.anchor: قدر لحدوث كل حادث أسبابا معينة وأوقاتا مقدرة يستحيل فيها التقدم والتأخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording depicts victory as longing for Muhammad: the promise already warrants it, and only a missing condition delayed its arrival.
rows.anchor: أن اللفظ دل على أن النصر كان كالمشتاق إلى محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī imagines God's mercy flowing from pre-eternity like a sea whose waves are now nearing Muhammad; when it arrives, he should sail it with glorification, praise, and forgiveness.
rows.anchor: بحار رحمة الله ونصرته كانت آخذة في السيلان من الأزل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These three devotions are the vessel for surviving the sea of divine lordship; Noah likewise invoked God's name as his ship moved and rested.
rows.anchor: فهذه الثلاثة هي السفينة التي لا يمكن الخلاص من بحار الربوبية إلا بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Companions' support is also God's victory: their motives and impulses are created by God, the ultimate cause, while each person is the proximate cause; a chain of divinely arranged causes answers the objection from conditional aid.
rows.anchor: وذلك لأن فعلهم فعل الله ، وتقريره أن أفعالهم مسندة إلى ما في قلوبهم من الدواعي والصوارف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says the future promise calls God “Allah,” while a past victory report calls Him “Lord,” because He is described as Lord after the act but was God before it.
rows.anchor: لأنه تعالى بعد وجود الفعل صار ربا ، وقبله ما كان ربا لكن كان إلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Muhammad supported God's religion and God promised support, victory becomes binding through the promise: divine generosity, mercy, sovereignty, providence, and uniqueness all ground that obligation.
rows.anchor: أن ما ليس بواجب قد يصير واجبا بالوعد ، ولهذا قيل : وعد الكريم ألزم من دين الغريم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the opening as the conquest of Mecca, called the conquest of conquests.
rows.anchor: نقل عن ابن عباس أن الفتح هو فتح مكة وهو الفتح الذي يقال له : فتح الفتوح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed report says that after Ḥudaybiyya, Quraysh's ally attacked the Prophet's ally Khuzaʿa; a messenger appealed to Muhammad, who predicted God's coming victory and expected Abū Sufyān to seek renewal of the treaty.
rows.anchor: أغار بعض من كان في عهد قريش على خزاعة وكانوا في عهد رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report says Sarah carried Ḥāṭib's warning letter to Mecca; ʿAlī and ʿAmmār recovered it, and Ḥāṭib said he sought protection for his family, not out of disbelief or affection for Quraysh.
rows.anchor: فخرجت سارة ونزل جبريل بالخبر ، فبعث رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عليا عليه السلام وعمارا

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: ʿUmar called Ḥāṭib a hypocrite and asked to kill him; Muhammad replied that God had looked upon the people of Badr and forgiven them, at which ʿUmar wept.
rows.anchor: فقال عمر : دعني أضرب عنق هذا المنافق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Marr al-Ẓahrān, ʿAbbās brought Abū Sufyān to Muhammad; after questioning Islam and prophethood, Abū Sufyān sought a pact to spare Mecca, and ʿAbbās warned him that ʿUmar might kill him.
rows.anchor: وقدم العباس وأبو سفيان إليه فاستأذنا فأذن لعمه خاصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad told Abū Sufyān that his supporters had protected and aided him, while Mecca's people expelled and wronged him; ʿAbbās then showed him the army, which he mistook for a great kingdom.
rows.anchor: هؤلاء نصروني وأعانوني وذبوا عن حريمي ، وأهل مكة أخرجوني وظلموني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report says Hind urged Meccans to kill Abū Sufyān; after hearing the Muslim call to dawn prayer and learning the army numbered ten thousand, he sought amnesty, and Muhammad granted safety to those who entered his house, the mosque, or laid down arms and stayed indoors.
rows.anchor: من دخل دار أبي سفيان فهو آمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad asked Mecca what they expected; they called him a generous brother and nephew, and he released them. The narrator says this is why Meccans were called “the released.”
rows.anchor: فقال : اذهبوا فأنتم الطلقاء فاعتقهم ، فلذلك سمي أهل مكة الطلقاء

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī later told Muʿāwiya that a patron and one set free are not equal, recalling that Muslims held Meccans' lives in their power and released them.
rows.anchor: أنى يستوي المولى والمعتق يعني اعتقناكم حين مكننا الله من رقابكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī explains “released ones” rather than “freed slaves” with wordplay: they might return to captivity, were kept in Mecca like divorced women at home, and were not free to depart.
rows.anchor: ولأن المعتق يخلى سبيله يذهب حيث شاء ، والمطلقة تجلس في البيت للعدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report says the Meccans pledged allegiance and entered Islam in groups; Muhammad prayed eight units, four as forenoon prayer and four as a voluntary prayer of thanks.
rows.anchor: روى أنه عليه السلام صلى ثمان ركعات : أربعة صلاة الضحى ، وأربعة أخرى شكرا لله نافلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators identify the opening with Mecca: Badr brought victory without conquest, and Banū al-Naḍīr brought conquest without decisive victory; at Mecca both came together.
rows.anchor: ومما يدل على أن المراد بالفتح فتح مكة أنه تعالى ذكره مقرونا بالنصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second view identifies the opening with Khaybar, conquered by ʿAlī; Rāzī begins a story contrasting ʿAlī's courage with Khālid's.
rows.anchor: القول الثاني : أن المراد فتح خيبر ، وكان ذلك على يد علي عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the conquest means Mecca, one chronology has the sūrah revealed two years after the conquest, with the Prophet living seventy days afterward; this earned it the name “the Farewell.”
rows.anchor: أن فتح مكة كان سنة ثمان ، ونزلت هذه السورة سنة عشر ، وروى أنه عاش بعد نزول هذه السورة سبعين يوما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second chronology places the sūrah before Mecca's conquest, making it a miraculous prediction; the future wording and the parallel promise of return support this reading.
rows.anchor: أن هذه السورة نزلت قبل فتح مكة ، وهو وعد لرسول الله أن ينصره على أهل مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article in “the opening” points to the previously known conquest of Mecca.
rows.anchor: الأولف واللام للمعهود السابق ، فينصرف إلى فتح مكة

none: Verse heading and text introduction only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You saw” can mean visual perception, making “entering” a circumstantial accusative, or knowledge, making the clause the second object of “knew.”
rows.anchor: رأيت يحتمل أن يكون معناه أبصرت ، وأن يكون معناه علمت

rows.speaker: الحسن بن علي
rows.claim: To explain why not every human entered Islam, al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī said the true people are his family, their adherents are their likenesses, and their enemies are lesser beings; ʿAlī affirmed his wisdom.
rows.anchor: وسئل الحسن بن علي عليه السلام . من الناس ؟ فقال : نحن الناس ، وأشياعنا أشباه الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says humanity's purpose is religion and obedience, so those who reject true religion are like cattle and are treated as though not truly human.
rows.anchor: أن المقصود من الإنسانية والعقل ، إنما هو الدين والطاعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The praise of late converts signals expansive mercy: even after a lifetime of unbelief, faith at the end is accepted and praised; long divine nurture makes the repentance especially welcome.
rows.anchor: فإن العبد بعد أن أتى بالكفر والمعصية طول عمره ، فإذا أتى بالإيمان في آخر عمره يقبل إيمانه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A prophetic report compares God's joy at a person's repentance to a lost traveler finding water; the author uses it to illustrate God's acceptance of late repentance.
rows.anchor: ويروى أنه عليه السلام قال : ( لله أفرح بتوبة أحدكم من الضال الواجد ، والظمآن الوارد )

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra reports that the “people” entering in crowds were Yemenites, whose hearts were tender and whose faith, jurisprudence, and wisdom were Yemeni; the Prophet sensed his Lord's help from Yemen.
rows.anchor: روى أن المراد بالناس أهل اليمن ، قال أبو هريرة : لما نزلت هذه السورة ، قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : ( الله أكبر جاء نصر الله والفتح

rows.speaker: جمهور الفقهاء وكثير من المتكلمين
rows.claim: Most jurists and many theologians hold that an imitator's faith is valid, since the converts praised here lacked detailed knowledge of sophisticated proofs about God, bodies, miracles, and prophetic truth.
rows.anchor: قال جمهور الفقهاء وكثير من المتكلمون : إن إيمان المقلد صحيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowing only some premises of a proof leaves its conclusion imitative; knowing all of them cannot be increased by extra detail, since either the added premise is necessary or irrelevant.
rows.anchor: فمن علم تسعة / منها ، وكان في المقدمة العاشرة مقلدا كان في النتيجة مقلدا لا محالة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reports that after Mecca fell, Arabs concluded Muhammad must be right because God protected the Sanctuary and its people from the army of the Elephant and other attackers; they then converted without fighting.
rows.anchor: إذا ظفر بأهل الحرم وجب أن يكون على الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because that inference from military victory is unsound, Rāzī concludes the Arab converts were imitators, supporting the validity of imitative faith.
rows.anchor: ومعلوم أن الاستدلال بأنه لما ظفر بأهل مكة وجب أن يكون على الحق ليس بجيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's religion is Islam, also called faith, the path, God's word and light, guidance, the firm handle, God's rope, His dye, and the innate disposition.
rows.anchor: دين الله هو الإسلام لقوله تعالى : { إن الدين عند الله الإسلام }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Religion of Allah” rather than “religion of the Lord” makes acceptance rest on God's identity and attributes, not gratitude for personal benefit, preserving sincerity.
rows.anchor: هذا الاسم أعظم الأسماء لدلالته على الذات والصفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A “fawj” is a large group: whole tribes entered after people had previously converted singly or in pairs.
rows.anchor: الفوج : الجماعة الكثيرة كانت تدخل فيه القبيلة بأسرها

rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh wept, recalling the Prophet's prediction that people would enter God's religion in groups and later leave in groups; he sought refuge from losing faith after receiving it.
rows.anchor: وعن جابر بن عبد الله أنه بكى ذات يوم فقيل له : ما يبكيك فقال : سمعت رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because delayed victory can prompt the thought that God favored falsehood, tasbīḥ first clears God of blame: for Rāzī, no one can obligate God; for the Muʿtazilites, delay reflects wisdom, not stinginess or bias.
rows.anchor: أما على قولنا : فالمراد من هذا التنزيه أنك منزه عن أن يستحق أحد عليك شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After declaring God free of fault, one praises His gifts and then seeks forgiveness for one's own sins.
rows.anchor: ثم إذا فرغ العبد عن تنزيه الله عما لا ينبغي فحينئذ يشتغل بحمده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī contrasts two contemplative paths: seeing God after created things and seeing Him before them; the latter is superior because reasoning from cause to effect is stronger than the reverse.
rows.anchor: فمنهم من قال : ما رأيت شيئا إلا ورأيت الله بعده ، ومنهم من قال : ما رأيت شيئا إلا ورأيت الله قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse follows the superior path by attending first to the Creator through glorification and praise, then turning to the self through forgiveness.
rows.anchor: قدم الاشتغال بالخالق على الاشتغال بالنفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine attributes divide into negative and affirmative; negation comes first, so glorification indicates majesty's negative attributes and praise indicates generosity's affirmative attributes.
rows.anchor: والسلوب مقدمة على الإيجابات فالتسبيح إشارة إلى التعرض للصفات السلبية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forgiveness combines awareness of one's shortcoming, God's generosity, and seeking what is best; it follows glorification and praise because attention to anything besides God veils His majesty.
rows.anchor: أن الاستغفار فيه رؤية قصور النفس ، وفيه رؤية جود الحق ، وفيه طلب لما هو الأصلح والأكمل للنفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command models angelic devotion: humanity's highest degree reaches the angels' lowest, and the angels say they glorify and sanctify God.
rows.anchor: إرشاد للبشر إلى التشبه بالملكية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possibility is that angels claim their own glorification, whereas Muhammad must attribute his worship to divine enabling and seek forgiveness for imagining it his own achievement.
rows.anchor: بل يجب أن تراها من توفيقي وإحساني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As angels seek forgiveness for believers, Muhammad should seek forgiveness for the crowds entering Islam, like the angels' prayer for those who repent and follow God's way.
rows.anchor: فأنت يا محمد استغفر للذين جاؤوا أفواجا كالملائكة يستغفرون للذين آمنوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tasbīḥ may mean purifying the Kaaba by breaking its idols; the Prophet should do so with God's praise and help, then admit his own shortcoming and seek forgiveness.
rows.anchor: الوجه الرابع : التسبيح هو التطهير ، فيحتمل أن يكون المراد طهر الكعبة من الأصنام وكسرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether or not Muhammad is sinless, he must continue servitude: glorification and praise if infallible, forgiveness if not, until death ends the obligation.
rows.anchor: فتكون الآية كالتنبيه على أنه لا فراغ عن التكليف في العبودية كما قال : { واعبد ربك حتى يأتيك اليقين }
